name: VoiceMOAT
tagline: A voice AI product: speech in, model in the middle, speech back out, wrapped in a hosted service.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The core loop of a voice agent, capture mic audio, transcribe it, send it to a model, speak the reply, is a genuinely short build now that streaming STT and TTS are commodity APIs. An agent can get you talking to your own thing in one sitting, and it will feel like magic for about ten minutes. Then you notice the turn-taking is clumsy, the interruptions do not work, and the round trip is a second and a half when it needs to be under five hundred milliseconds. Latency budgeting, barge-in, endpointing and phone-network plumbing are where the real engineering lives, and none of that is one-shot territory. Build it if you want a personal voice interface to your own stuff; do not build it if you need something that answers a phone number reliably.
coreLoopDIY: A local web page plus server that streams your microphone to a speech-to-text API, feeds the transcript to an LLM with a system prompt and tool calls, and streams synthesized speech back with interruption support.
requirements: API keys for a streaming STT provider, an LLM, and a TTS provider
A machine or small VPS that can stay running
A browser with microphone access over HTTPS or localhost
Tolerance for per-minute usage costs while you test
No phone number: browser only, unless you add a telephony provider
whatYouLose: Sub-second end-to-end latency that took someone months of tuning
Telephony: inbound and outbound calls, SIP trunks, DTMF, call recording
Robust barge-in and endpointing, so callers can interrupt without breaking the flow
Dashboards, transcripts, call analytics and evaluation of whether the agent actually did its job
Uptime you would bet a customer conversation on
moatNotes: Voice is a latency product. The demo is easy, the last 300 milliseconds and the 3am failure modes are the whole business.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a voice agent that mostly works is worse than no voice agent at all, and getting from mostly to reliably is unglamorous work: tuning endpointing so it does not talk over people, handling half-duplex phone audio, retrying a dead TTS stream mid sentence, keeping p95 latency flat when the model provider gets slow. If voice is a side quest for you, a hosted service absorbs that. If it is a hobby project talking to you in your kitchen, pay nobody and build it yourself.
notes: Personal voice interfaces are now a weekend; production voice is still a team.
prompt:
Build a local, self-hosted voice agent I can talk to in my browser. No accounts, no cloud database, no telemetry.

Stack, non-negotiable:
- Python 3.11 with FastAPI and a single WebSocket endpoint
- Vanilla HTML/JS front end served from the same app, no build step
- Deepgram streaming STT, OpenAI for the LLM, ElevenLabs streaming TTS
- All keys read from .env via python-dotenv; ship .env.example, never commit .env
- uv or plain venv plus requirements.txt, your call, but pick one and document it

Behaviour:
1. Browser page with one big Talk button. Capture mic audio with getUserMedia, downsample to 16kHz PCM, stream it over the WebSocket in small chunks.
2. Server pipes audio to Deepgram streaming transcription with interim results enabled. Show interim text live on the page.
3. On a final transcript with an end-of-speech signal, append it to a conversation history and call the LLM with streaming enabled and a system prompt loaded from prompt.txt.
4. Send LLM output to ElevenLabs streaming TTS sentence by sentence as tokens arrive, and stream the audio back over the same WebSocket. Play it in the browser with an AudioWorklet or MediaSource, not one giant blob at the end.
5. Barge-in: if new speech is detected while audio is playing, stop playback immediately, cancel the in-flight LLM and TTS requests, and start a new turn.
6. Two tool calls the LLM can use: get_time and a local_notes tool that appends a line to notes.md. Wire the tool loop properly.
7. Log each turn to a JSONL file with timestamps for mic-stop, transcript-final, first-LLM-token, first-audio-byte, so I can actually see my latency budget. Print the breakdown to the console after every turn.

Explicitly out of scope: phone calls, SIP, user auth, multi-tenant anything, Docker, a database, a mobile app.

Deliver a README with setup in under ten commands and one paragraph on which step is the slowest and what I could do about it.
